Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00373

Any whole made of joined parts, such as a human being, includes a higher part—the soul—and a lower part—the body's matter. There must be a fitting link between them, and between each part and that link. The human being therefore has many powers. Some take things in; others move us to act. The powers of perception include intellect, inner judgment, imagination, and the senses. They differ in strength and in how much they depend on matter. Intellect is least tied to matter, followed by inner judgment, imagination, and the senses. The five senses also differ: touch is most tied to matter, then taste, smell, hearing, and sight.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00374

Each of these eight kinds has its own range of strength and weakness. The powers that move us—anger, desire, and the powers of plant life—also differ in how much they depend on matter. The more a power depends on matter, the more it can be divided. The less it depends on matter, the less divided it is. The soul itself cannot be split in its immaterial nature, but through its connection to the body it can be described as divided.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00375

The great philosopher says that the soul is divided only indirectly. When it is in a body, it is divided along with the body. We can speak of its thinking part as distinct from its animal part, or its desiring part from its angry part. The soul itself is not divided; the body it inhabits is. When we say that the soul is divided, we mean that it is present in each part of the body and is divided along with it. The body's organs show this: an organ can sense only because a power of the soul is present in it. Since the soul's power of sensation is present in all the sense organs, it is called divided along with them. Yet it is complete in every organ. It is not split as the organs are. It is divided only in the way just described.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00376

These many powers are gathered together in the soul but spread throughout the body. They are spread out because each needs a suitable organ. An organ that serves sight, for example, cannot serve hearing in the same way. The bodily place suited to anger is not the one suited to desire. Touch is the lowest and least refined power, close to the most basic qualities of matter, so many organs can serve it.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00377

The philosopher says that each power has a particular place in the body. It does not need that place in order to exist; it needs it so that it can act through a part prepared for its work. The soul prepares an organ in the way needed for a power to act through it. Its powers differ according to the differences among the organs. But the soul is not made up of separate powers. It is one and simple, and it continually gives powers to the body. Since the soul causes these powers, their qualities belong more properly to the soul than to the body, especially when they are qualities better suited to the soul. The soul's powers must have places in the body. Otherwise, there would be no difference between being inside the body and being outside it. The body's movement and sensation would have nothing to do with the soul, and we could not explain how the soul acts through bodily organs.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00378

How can powers whose existence keeps changing still belong, as one and the same individual, to one personal soul? The answer is that changing things remain one through a single, unified reality, as the body is held together by the soul and matter by its form. Matter and form make one being; so do soul and body. The soul completes the body, and a thing's completion is that thing in a fuller and stronger way. Each lower power, as it changes, keeps its identity through a higher power that remains stable and is its source. This continues up the scale until we reach something fixed in every way.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00379

This also answers a problem about touch. Touch works only when the part of the body that touches is changed from its usual state by receiving a quality opposite to the quality it senses. It seems, then, that the first quality must disappear when the opposite one arrives. Since sensation depends on the sense's power, that power should disappear too. But perception requires the image perceived to remain.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00380

The answer is that the lowest power of touch may disappear and be replaced by another like it. The power of perception above it gathers what came before: it uses the earlier state to perceive the later one and holds them together, even when the earlier state has passed away.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00381

The philosopher divides the soul's powers into two kinds. Some are divided along with the body, such as growth and desire, which extend throughout a plant or animal. A higher power gathers these divided powers together. A power that is spread through the body can therefore be undivided in the higher power above it. The bodily senses are spread among separate organs, but one inner sense gathers them together. It receives what the senses report and recognizes and compares their reports at once. This inner sense is not divided because it does not act through a bodily organ. Its greater freedom from matter allows it to take in and distinguish all the sensed things together.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00382

I say that this is a valuable insight. It helps explain many things: how bodies are raised in the afterlife; how what we know remains connected to its causes; and how a person remains the same through change from one moment to the next. Avicenna could not grasp this, despite his quick mind and sharp understanding. When Bahmanyār asked whether the self could change, Avicenna replied, “I do not have to answer you, since I will not be held to account when you ask me.”
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00383

These subtle truths cannot be reached by memorizing rules and definitions alone. They require inner insight and direct spiritual experience. Such insight comes through spiritual practice and effort in solitude, with distance from other people and from worldly desires, ambitions, and false hopes. Much of this philosopher's writing shows his deep insight, inner light, and closeness to God. He may have taken up worldly duties—governing, improving people's lives, and building cities—after completing his spiritual practice and perfecting himself, when no one concern distracted him from another. He may have wanted to unite worldly leadership with spiritual leadership, and to complete both forms of life.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00384

He then taught people, helped them improve, and guided them toward the right path, seeking closeness to God. Avicenna did not take up worldly affairs in this way. It is striking that whenever his inquiry turned to the nature of existence itself, rather than general questions and rules, his understanding seemed to fail him. This happened in many places. For example, he rejected change in the very nature of a thing. He thought that if Zayd changed in his humanity, he would have to stop being human and become something else. Yet any change requires something to remain through it. He missed the different ways one nature can exist, some more complete than others, and how one person can pass through many levels of being. If existence were only an idea we drew from things, as many later thinkers believed, Avicenna would have been right. But existence is not merely an idea.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00385

He also rejected Plato's forms that exist apart from matter. He rejected the idea that the knower and what is known can be one, and that the soul can be one with the Active Intellect. He could not accept the idea that basic matter longs for form, or that the forms of the elements can change into a single, balanced form. He could not prove that bodies are raised in the afterlife. He also believed that the heavens and stars had always existed as individual things, each with its own form, matter, size, shape, color, and light. He thought that their movements and positions had existed forever only as kinds, not as individual movements. He also believed that the matter of earthly things had always existed, though we have already shown that it began to exist.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00386

Bahmanyār once asked Avicenna why some powers of the soul can perceive while others cannot, even though all belong to one self. Avicenna replied, “I have not worked this out.” In his writing about the soul, Avicenna had already said that it thinks, imagines, senses, and moves. Bahmanyār also asked whether Avicenna could identify something that stayed the same in animals and plants. “If only I could,” Avicenna replied. He was asked whether animals other than humans are aware of themselves. He said he would have to think about it. Perhaps they are aware only of what they sense or imagine, not of themselves; perhaps they know themselves through bodily tools; or perhaps they have a shared kind of awareness among their inner images.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00387

I have explained earlier that animals with active imagination do not have material souls. They know themselves in a particular way, because their existence belongs to them and not to something else. Whatever exists in itself, rather than in another thing, is aware of itself. This does not mean animal souls are intellectual beings. Being free of matter does not always mean being an intellect.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00388

A related question asks: if an animal power can know that it should flee from a wolf, or that something is dangerous, why can it not know general ideas? These ideas also have no size and cannot exist in a body.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00389

Avicenna's answer was that fear and flight become intellectual only after a certain kind of separation from matter. This does not answer the question. Fear, flight, desire, anger, love, and similar states are meanings that cannot be divided. They are not things with size, shape, or position. How, then, can they exist in a body or in a power that itself depends on a body? Their condition before they are separated from matter is already like that of many things after they are separated. The right answer is that the power that knows these simple meanings must be an animal power that is not located in a body. It need not be an intellect.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00390

Avicenna was also asked how a thing can become an intellect when universal forms come to be in it. This seemed strange: how could something that is not yet an intellect be made into one by receiving a form that makes it an intellect? Avicenna said that “becomes” did not mean it changed at that moment; it only showed that the thing was already an intellect.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00391

I say that Avicenna gave the word this strained meaning because he believed that the human soul is an intellect free of matter from the moment it begins in the fourth month of pregnancy. But as I explained earlier, the soul does not begin that way. At first, imagination is active and intellect is only a possibility. Through repeated perception, the soul draws general ideas from particular images and moves from a possible intellect to an active one. Its very nature changes as it passes from imaginative power to intellectual power. The many statements by ancient philosophers on this subject are clear and cannot be dismissed as metaphor.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00392
In one of his letters to a student, Avicenna writes:
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00393

“I have thought deeply about this problem. It is new to me. I have answered some parts with a convincing argument and others only by hint. I may have failed to answer some. A stable principle in animals is easier to explain, and I have explored it at length in the Eastern studies, first by raising doubts and then by seeking insight. But the case of plants is harder.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00394

“If nothing stable remains in a plant, then its identity is not a kind but an individual. But how can it remain the same individual if its change can be divided endlessly in thought, with no one division more basic than another? How can infinitely many changes happen in a limited time?
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00395

“Perhaps the matter is what remains. But how can matter stay the same when its size keeps changing? Growth does not happen in one matter alone; new matter enters through nourishment. Perhaps one plant form can take in and wear more than one portion of matter. But how can one form belong to just one portion of matter?
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00396

“Perhaps one form stays with one portion of matter for the whole life of the individual. But how can that be, when the parts of a growing thing increase alike? Each similar part becomes larger than before. The power is present everywhere in the body, so no one part has a stronger claim than another to be the original form.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00397

“Perhaps the earliest power is the original one that remains. But its relation to the earlier stage is like the relation of a later stage to the next. Perhaps a plant is not really one individual in number: each part added at one time is a new individual, joined to the first. Or perhaps the first part is the source from which a second, similar one comes. When the first disappears, the second then disappears too. Perhaps this applies to animals, or to most animals, but not to plants, since they cannot divide into parts that can live on their own.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00398

“Or perhaps an animal or plant has a root that is not mixed with its body, though the body is mixed. But this would go against what I believe. Perhaps what seems alike to the senses is not alike in reality. Or perhaps a plant is never one individual, except during the pause in growth that must occur at times. These are puzzles and traps. If the mind circles around them, branches into them, and examines their different sides, I hope it will find a way out, by God's help, toward the truth.”
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00399

I say that these alternatives show that Avicenna could not explain how a plant—or even an animal—can grow in size and still remain the same individual. He could not identify something stable in them through change, because he thought their souls were part of their bodily matter. But it is striking that one of his possible answers was the truth: an animal or plant has a source that is not mixed with its body. This is certain for animals, since they have a soul distinct from the body. It is also true of plants, whose changing powers depend on a stable power above them.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00400

We have also shown that an indefinite amount of matter is included in the identity of a natural being with a complete form. Because matter enters this identity only in an undefined way, changes in the body's size do not break the person's identity.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00401

Avicenna also struggled with whether simple human souls survive the body. Since he could not prove that imagination is free of matter, he sometimes said that such souls cease to exist, although he accepted that a nonphysical substance does not perish when a body does. At other times, he said they survive by knowing a few first principles and general truths. But anyone with a firm grounding in philosophy knows that the next life is a life of knowledge. Rational souls have their being through understanding intellectual realities. A thing cannot exist as a mere general idea: it must have its own definite reality. What happiness could the soul find in grasping only the idea of a thing or of possibility, whether taken in its broad or narrow sense, or in knowing that a whole is greater than its part and that things equal to the same thing are equal to one another? In this world, nothing exists merely as “substance in general” or “quality in general.” It must be a definite kind with its own form. The same is true in the world of intellect: nothing can exist there merely as “some thing,” “some possibility,” or “some substance” without becoming a distinct intellectual reality.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00402

Avicenna claimed that celestial souls have no further perfection to reach except an easier goal: gaining spatial relations to their bodies. To a thoughtful observer, this is a weak and mistaken view. As long as the soul is incomplete, it needs a body as a tool to reach its perfection. It uses and moves the body so that it can become more complete in its very being, not to gain some extra relation outside itself. How could a clear-thinking person believe that an intellectual soul is trapped in a body and has left the world of light for the world of darkness just to gain spatial relations? Avicenna himself says that higher beings do not turn their attention toward lower ones.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00403

Avicenna rejected the idea that a thing can change in its very nature. Yet he agreed that when the soul is complete and free of the body, it becomes an intellect and is no longer called a soul. He did not see that being a soul is not an added relation, like being a king or a ship's captain. The soul's very mode of existence makes it a soul. When its existence grows stronger and it becomes an intellect, its mode of existence changes. This is precisely a deep change in what it is—the kind of change he rejected.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00404

He also failed to understand the simple intellect. He said it means knowing many ideas all at once, without moving from one idea to another in time, but in an order of causes and effects. He quoted himself in Notes:
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00405

“Simple intellect means grasping all ideas at once, in their proper order and through their causes, without moving from one idea to another as the soul does when it learns them one by one. It knows each thing together with the causes that lead to it. If we say that the First has intellect in this simple sense, we mean that it knows things through their causes and sources, which are present to it because things come from it. We do not mean that the ideas of things are parts of its essence. Rather, the ideas flow from it, and it is more properly called intellect than the ideas that flow from its act of knowing.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00406

“Simple ideas are present to it all at once in their order: each is related to the ones before and after it, and to the First. Here is an example. You read a book, and someone asks whether you know what it contains. You say yes because you know its contents and can explain them in detail. This is what simple intellect means. There is no human intellect like this, except perhaps that of a prophet. Intellectual knowledge is not laid out in time; knowledge through the soul is.”
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00407

Avicenna repeated this account in Notes, but he did not go beyond the idea that our knowledge comes in a sequence in time, while the First's knowledge follows the order of causes and effects. He did not understand that a simple intellect can contain every intelligible without being divided.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00408

He also denied that separate intellectual forms could be God's detailed knowledge of things. He thought these forms were separate from God and had a different nature. If so, how could they be necessary to God? And if they were not necessary, something else would have to come before them and produce them, leading to an endless chain. He therefore treated God's knowledge as qualities that exist within Him, though he said that they neither affect Him nor make Him more complete.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00409

You have already seen the error in this view. The intellectual forms are not separate beings that exist apart from God. These and similar mistakes come from overlooking what existence is and how it works, and from spending time on subjects that are not needed for this path: grammar, detailed arithmetic, music, the many treatments used in medicine, lists of simple drugs and mixtures, antidotes, poisons, ointments, laxatives, and the treatment of sores and wounds. God made different people for different fields; the person seeking God should not lose themselves in all these details.
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00410

When Socrates was asked why he turned away from the practical sciences, he replied, “I am occupied with the noblest science”—meaning the knowledge of God. In short, for someone with a clear mind, a gentle nature, sharp intelligence, sound judgment, and strong ability, the key is to avoid worldly concerns and the pursuit of status. They must turn from people, seek solitude, find ease in God, and place their attention and thought on divine realities. First they need some knowledge of language, logic, nature, and character—enough for those who seek God through study, though not for those drawn to Him from the start by a divine pull as strong as the efforts of all people together. Without either path, how could someone reach inner insight into God, the beginning and end of all things, the soul, and its journey to God while caught up in worldly ties?
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00411
Avicenna says in a letter to a student who asked him to rewrite a book that had been lost during one of his journeys:
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00412

“Who is this person forced to begin again, to move from falsehood to truth, from this world to the next, from empty details to what matters? Fate has caught me in its claws. I do not know how to escape. I have been given tasks that do not suit me. I have lost touch with knowledge; I can only glimpse it through a thick curtain. Still, I thank God: through changing conditions, great trials, and repeated journeys, He never leaves me without a flash of light that gives my heart life and steadies my steps. I praise Him for what helps and harms, what grieves and delights.”
Book Nine: The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00413

I say: Even if these duties had been forced on Avicenna, without his choosing them, who wrote so much about particular sciences and crafts? Did his deep immersion in them not keep him from turning toward God, staying close to Him, and seeking greater light and knowledge from Him?
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00414
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00415
I. What true happiness is
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00416

Existence is good and a source of happiness. Being aware of existence is also good and brings happiness. But beings differ in how complete they are. The more complete a being's existence, the less it is marked by absence and limitation, and the greater its happiness. The less complete its existence, the more evil and misery are mixed into it. The First Reality, God, is the most complete and noble of all. Below God are the intellects free of bodies, then souls. Lower still are natural powers and bodily forms. At the lowest level are basic matter, time, and motion.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00417

Each thing finds pleasure in existing. It would find even greater pleasure in existing through its own cause and what completes it, since that is the source of its being. The more complete a being is, the greater its happiness, which comes from awareness of its existence. The intellectual powers exist at a higher level than the animal powers of desire and anger, so their happiness, pleasure, and love are greater. When our souls become complete and strong, break free of their ties to the body, and return to their true selves and their Creator, their joy will be beyond description and beyond comparison with bodily pleasures.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00418

The causes of pleasure are awareness, the thing perceived, and the power of perception. Awareness of a thing is stronger when the perceiving power is stronger, and when the thing perceived is more complete. The intellect is stronger than the senses, and its objects are more complete. It reaches the true nature of what it understands and attains pure light, good, and being—the source of all that exists and of all goodness. The intellectual beings that follow God are also beautiful and beloved in themselves, whether anyone else loves them or not.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00419

Sensory perception, by contrast, comes through powers that are weaker and less complete. It reaches only the outer parts of things, not their full nature. The senses perceive food, touch, smells, colors, and similar things. Intellect can know all things; the senses know only some things, and only those that can be sensed. Not every sensed thing is pleasant, but everything understood by the mind is suited to the intellect and completes it. Sensible things can conflict with one another because they are limited and can be harmed. Intellectual beings have room to exist without crowding one another.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00420

When the intellect understands an intellectual form, it becomes more complete through that form. In a sense, the form becomes part of what the intellect is. Some of these forms were already present as part of the intellect's nature, but it had not noticed them because it was occupied elsewhere. When it turns inward and becomes aware of them, it sees beauty and splendor in itself. As the First Teacher says: “I went within myself and left all other things behind. There I found a beauty and splendor that words cannot describe.”
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00421

This pleasure resembles the joy the First Reality has in itself, and the joy of those close to God in themselves and in their source. The angels' joy in their spiritual awareness is greater than a donkey's joy in mating or eating. While we are tied to our bodies, however, we do not feel or desire these higher pleasures as we feel bodily ones. We learn about them through proof. We know the beloved intellectual beings only through general ideas that apply to them, but an idea of a thing is not its actual existence. The idea of sweetness is not sweet. Knowing what kingship is does not make you a king.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00422

Reason and proof tell us that these intellectual pleasures exist, and that knowing them in this life prepares us to experience them in the next. Knowledge is the seed of direct vision. What blocks us from intellectual beings is either that we have not learned about them, or that we are too busy with the body, material things, and the powers tied to them. The soul can approach these beings by learning what they are. As its knowledge becomes firmer, it becomes ready to receive their forms from the intellect that does not depend on a body. When the soul is separated from the body at death, it no longer turns toward bodily concerns. Its knowledge then gives it access to what it knows, and it takes pleasure in it.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00423

Bodily perception is different. Seeing a pleasant object does not always bring pleasure, because a physical body may be blocked from reaching it. The parts of a body are separate, and the body is not fully present to itself or to anything else. The qualities and states that depend on a body are limited in the same way. A body, simply by being a body, is not alive or aware. A living body is alive because something else in it—the animal soul—is alive in itself. If bodily existence itself were life, every body would be alive. A being that is not a body, even if connected to a body, can have life simply by existing. This is true of God, the intellects, and the souls of the celestial bodies, humans, and animals. Life is not something added to existence; life is existence itself. The same holds for place and relation in a body, and for light in immaterial beings.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00424

The point of this discussion is that bodily existence always carries death, distraction, separation, and loss, whether on the side of the perceiver or the thing perceived. The more a being depends on a body, the less present it is to itself and to other things, and the weaker its awareness becomes. We were more aware of ourselves before we became attached to our bodies. Most people, lost in their material bodies and concerns, forget themselves—as God says, “They forgot God, so He made them forget themselves.” Our sense of self while we are tied to the body is mixed with our awareness of it, because soul and body are joined like light and shadow, flame and smoke, or a person and their reflection.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00425

When the soul's tie to the body ends, it sees intellectual forms directly. Awareness becomes presence, knowledge becomes direct sight, and perception becomes inward vision. The pleasure of intellectual life is greater than any other good or happiness. As we have seen, true pleasure comes from existence, especially intellectual existence, which is free from the trace of nonexistence. The truest beloved and fullest perfection is God, who is existence itself and contains every kind of being. Joy in God is the greatest joy and rest: it is rest without pain.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00426
II. How the soul reaches this happiness, and why it is kept from it in this world
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00427

The soul reaches this joy and happiness through actions that purify it, clear away its inner stains, and polish the mirror of the heart. It also reaches them through thought and study that help it understand the forms and natures of things. When the soul has learned what things are and its intellect has become active, it no longer needs the senses, body, or bodily powers. Yet the body and its powers still distract it and keep it from full union with the intellect and from reaching its source.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00428

When the body's demands, the whispering of inner judgment, and the play of imagination fall away, the barrier lifts and union continues. The soul remains; the active source remains; its giving is constant; and the soul is ready to receive it. Both barriers—the inner one and the outer one—must be removed. The inner barrier is the soul's weakness and potential state, and its deep entanglement with the body. It is removed when the soul becomes actual in its own intellectual nature and clearly distinguishes itself from the body and its powers. The outer barrier is the body and its senses, like a cover around a polished mirror. It is removed when the soul leaves the body at death.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00429

The body and senses are needed at first. Through them, the soul gains sound images and learns to draw general meanings from them, waking to its own world, its source, and its return. At the beginning of life, the soul can recognize truths only through the senses. That is why people say, “Whoever loses a sense loses knowledge.” The senses help at first but hold us back at the end, like a fishing net or a mount that carries us to our destination. Once we arrive, the very thing that helped us can become a distraction.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00430

Each power is happy when it gets what suits its nature, without an obstacle, and reaches its full strength. Desire is fulfilled when it gets what it wants; anger when it wins or takes revenge; inner judgment when it hopes and imagines what might be. Each sense is fulfilled by the quality it can perceive. Touch perceives a balanced bodily state; taste perceives flavors suited to the body, such as sweetness and richness; smell takes in pleasant scents; sight, light and color; hearing, harmonious sounds and pleasing melodies. Imagination forms pleasing images, either from sense images or from intellectual meanings presented through images. The intellect, in its own nature, reaches pure intellectual realities and receives the divine forms and the order of all that exists, from the First Reality down to the lowest beings.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00431

The soul's happiness through its link to the body and its life in this world comes from justice. It must act in a balanced way between opposing traits—between what it wants and does not want, and between anger and restraint—so that it is not controlled by the body and its powers. While the soul remains in this world, it cannot be entirely free of the body's influence. But balance makes it act as if it were free of that influence. It does not give in to the body's powers. Instead, it rises above them, directs them, and makes them obey. Giving in to the body and being shaped by its powers brings misery and blocks happiness. At first, the soul and body affect one another. Sometimes the soul overcomes the body, with God's help. At other times, the soul gives in to bodily powers, led astray by Satan through the tricks of inner judgment and the body's desires. If the soul gives in again and again, it becomes deeply shaped by the body and forms a bad habit. Then it is harder to resist the body's harms than it was before.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00432

If the soul repeatedly restrains the body and rises above its demands, it gains inner strength and finds it easier to do what once was hard. This strength comes from acting with balance in the ways the body requires while we live in it, without excess or neglect. A person becomes weak and submissive by going to extremes. Balanced actions, by contrast, leave the soul free from bodily control. They are like water that is neither hot nor cold. This inner strength suits the soul's nature. The soul is naturally drawn to being independent and free of matter; obedience to bodily desires is foreign to its rational nature. The soul's true happiness and completion lie in independent, immaterial existence, in knowing things as they are, and in seeing intellectual realities and beings of light. These pleasures cannot be compared with the dim, passing pleasures of the senses and bodily desires.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00433

Why do we fail to enjoy the knowledge we already have? It is like an illness that dulls the sense of taste. The person cannot enjoy sweet or tasty things that are there for them. If the mind could hold the truths proper to it while free from bodily distractions and the pull of the senses, its pleasure would be beyond description. Those who know the truth do not feel a strong desire for these pleasures now because they do not yet fully taste them. True pleasure comes from the actual presence of something suited to us, not from an idea or a thought of it. What we have in the soul now is only a weak mental form of intellectual knowledge. Its weakness may come from bodily distraction, or from the weakness of the knowledge itself, such as knowledge based on guesswork rather than proof. But the realities themselves are strong, clear, and bright.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00434

If the soul's knowledge is weak only because the body clouds it—not because the soul has failed to understand or lacks sound proof—then once the body's veil is removed, that knowledge can lead the soul to see the beings brought close to God and be with them. Full knowledge in this life is the seed of full vision in the next. A soul that has gained true knowledge and is free of bad traits may also take on the pleasant forms promised in revelation—not as empty daydreams, but as forms shaped by its good actions and character. This is the paradise of those who live well without reaching full perfection, and the happiness of the righteous. The paradise of the perfected and those brought near to God is of a higher kind. In short, joy follows vision. The less clearly we see, the less joy we feel. This is also true of the happiness we know about but cannot yet see for ourselves.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00435

We can tell that higher happiness is real from the joy we feel when we remember God, reflect on His qualities and acts, and understand the order of existence as the best and most complete order. This points to a happiness we can reach when bodily concerns fall away. Our happiness will be greater still if we understand these questions fully, as those firmly grounded in knowledge do.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00436

At a minimum, to deserve this true happiness, a person should learn about the highest source of being, the kind of existence that belongs to it, and how it knows all things without being changed by them. A person should learn how it can do all that can be done without changing or becoming many, how it cares for all things, and how its mercy and generosity reach them. Its true qualities do not add to its being, though its relations to things do. Names such as the All-Powerful, the All-Knowing, the Provider, and the Creator are different ways of speaking about one simple relation. Just as all God's true qualities refer to the fullness of existence, all these other names refer to His being the complete source of all that exists.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00437

A person should also know the intellects that bring other beings into existence, God's complete and everlasting words, and His angels of knowledge; and the universal souls, which are His books and angels of action. They should understand the order by which existence flows from God to intellect, then to souls and natural powers, down to matter and bodies; and how existence rises again through minerals, plants, and animals to the acquired intellect, returning to where it began. Whoever gains this knowledge has won a great victory and a large share of happiness. They escape the misery that comes from turning away from knowledge despite having the ability and readiness to learn, from turning away from wisdom while wanting to gain knowledge, or from denying these truths out of arrogance and stubbornness. The more complete this knowledge becomes, the greater the person's happiness. I know people who have studied this field so deeply that they understand aspects of existence beyond the reach of even sharp minds, and unlike anything written by earlier or later philosophers. Praise and thanks be to God.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00438

We have seen that true nobility and happiness come to the soul through its theoretical side, which is the root of its being. What comes from its practical side, which is tied to the body and its needs, brings safety from hardship, purification from faults and stains, clarity instead of weakness and vice, and freedom from punishment and painful torment. By itself, though, this does not bring the soul true nobility or intellectual joy. Still, the righteous and those who live simply have a kind of happiness suited to them, as we will explain later.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00439
III. Misery opposed to true happiness
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00440

This kind of misery does not belong to animal souls, to souls that remain simple, or to ordinary people who have not yet developed a desire to learn the intellectual and theological sciences or a love of status and leadership. Most people who earn their living through crafts, ordinary people, women, and children fall into these groups. If they suffer, their suffering is of another kind; if they are happy, their happiness is of another kind too. Those who suffer fall into two groups. The first are those who were destined to go astray and against whom the decree was set from eternity. They belong to darkness, worldly life, and a veil that seals their hearts by nature. God says, “I will surely fill Hell with jinn and people,” and, “We have created many jinn and people for Hell. They have hearts with which they do not understand.”
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00441

The second group are hypocrites. They were originally able to receive the light of knowledge, but they strayed from the path. Their hearts grew veiled by stains they acquired through bad habits, wrongdoing, animal desires, and cruel impulses. They kept turning to the devil's tricks until dark ways of acting took root in them. Their minds filled with false arguments, mistaken ideas, empty images, and lies. They were left doubtful, lost, and turned away from the truth. Their actions came to nothing, and their souls were bound in painful misery, chained to matter and lost in the darkness of worldly desire. They had lost the powers and tools that once let them pursue these desires, and now they were stung by the scorpions and snakes of their own bad character. They would remain there as long as the heavens and earth endure. The call of truth had reached them, but they ignored it, went astray, turned away, and denied it. God's anger fell on them. It was said of them:
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00442

“Whoever turns away from My reminder will have a cramped life, and We will raise him blind on the Day of Resurrection. He will say, ‘My Lord, why have You raised me blind when I could see?’ He will say, ‘This is how Our signs came to you, but you forgot them; so today you are forgotten.’”
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00443

One of their greatest pains is that they are kept from their Lord. Their hearts are covered by what they did, their sins surround them, and they remain in the lowest part of the Fire. These people are in a worse state than the first group: the first are veiled from the truth, while the second are punished. The Qur'an speaks often of both groups and of each one separately. One example appears at the start of the chapter of the Cow. The first group is described in the words, “Those who disbelieve—it is the same to them whether you warn them or not,” through to, “They will have a terrible punishment.” They have no way out of the Fire; they are truly its companions. Their nature has been strengthened by repeated sin and desire. This is what is meant by, “Your Lord's word has come true against those who rebel: they will not believe,” and, “Your Lord's word has come true against those who disbelieve: they are the companions of the Fire.”
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00444

They have been shut off from the path and every door has been closed to them. The heart—the power of reason—is the inner sense where inspiration and guidance are received. Their hearts have been sealed, so they are cut off from it. The senses, especially hearing and sight, are two great doors to understanding and reflection. But these too have lost their use, because meaning can no longer reach the heart through them. They have no way to reach true knowledge inwardly.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00445

Nor can they gain the outward, conventional kinds of knowledge. The Qur'an says, “We have created many jinn and people for Hell. They have hearts with which they do not understand.” They are imprisoned in darkness. How great their pain is. The second group is described in the words, “Some people say, ‘We believe in God and the Last Day,’” through to, “They will have a terrible punishment.” Their hearts are sick and their souls suffer from resentment, envy, pride, hypocrisy, hatred, foolishness, and showing off. They are given to scheming, betrayal, deceit, discord, and manipulation. They may also hold false views and beliefs. God protect us: they may memorize religious teachings and formal knowledge, then use them to gain status and power, claiming to believe in God and the Last Day though faith has never entered their hearts. Whether or not these inner sicknesses involve false beliefs, they all cause pain to the soul and torment to the heart. False beliefs and corrupt knowledge cause even greater torment. They burn within the people who hold them, and their pain is worse than that of the fire of this world. God says, “It is God's kindled fire, which rises over the hearts; it will close in on them, in towering columns.” These beliefs are painful in themselves, and they also lead to other sins that torment the soul for a time. Both kinds are forms of intellectual misery. The bodily forms of happiness and misery will be explained later, God willing.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00446

To sum up, afterlife misery comes either from bodily habits formed by sins of desire and anger, or from inner habits such as envy, showing off, denying the truth, and rejecting true knowledge. The first kind forms when repeated surrender to bodily impulses becomes fixed. It keeps the soul from reaching its happiness in the afterlife and blocks it from its reward. It also causes pain because the soul loses the familiar things it longed for and has no distraction to keep it from remembering them. While the soul is turned toward the body, this attention keeps it from feeling how ugly these habits are and how much they oppose its true nature. In the afterlife, when that distraction ends, the soul feels their pain. God says, “We have lifted your veil, and today your sight is sharp.” When the veil is lifted at death, the soul feels great pain, like someone who has a painful illness but is too distracted to notice it; once the distraction is gone, the full pain becomes clear. These habits are foreign to the soul's true nature, as are the hellish forms that grow from them. So, God willing, they may fade over time, in a period that depends on how many obstacles remain. This may be what the true religion points to when it says that a sinful believer will not remain in the Fire forever.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00447

The second kind of intellectual misery is a deep, painful disease. A person may be able to learn and long for intellectual knowledge and completion, yet fail to make the effort needed to develop the intellect. The soul then loses its natural readiness and takes on twisted habits and false ideas that oppose reality. It speaks from stubborn loyalty to a view and denies what is true. This is a disease that even the doctors of the soul struggle to cure. What is impossible cannot be achieved. The pain it causes is the opposite of the pleasure that comes from intellectual completion. That pleasure is greater than any bodily pleasure; this pain is worse than any bodily pain, whether burning in fire, freezing in bitter cold, beheading, or losing a limb. People in this world may not feel it for the reason already explained: they do not feel its opposite pleasure either. Children do not understand the pleasures and pains known to mature adults. They may laugh at adults, enjoy what is not truly pleasant, and dislike what adults enjoy. The immature in understanding are like children in this respect.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00448
IV. Why some souls lack intellectual knowledge and miss happiness in the afterlife
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00449

The part of a person that receives knowledge is a subtle power that guides the body's organs and puts its senses and abilities to work. By its nature, it can receive every kind of knowledge, just as a mirror can reflect any color or visible thing. But five things can prevent it from receiving these forms of knowledge, as one scholar explains through the example of a mirror.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00450

The first is that the soul is not yet developed enough. A child's soul cannot clearly receive knowledge because it is still weak and only has the potential to know. This is like an iron mirror before it has been melted, shaped, and polished.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00451

The second is that the soul has become cloudy and dark. Desires and the layers built up through repeated sin block the heart's clarity and keep truth from appearing in it. This is like rust or dirt on a mirror. Every action leaves a mark on the soul. Actions driven by desire or anger hold it back from the perfection it could reach; acts of thought help it grow. Every time the soul is caught up in bodily, worldly concerns, it is like a dark spot on a mirror. When these spots gather, they distort the mirror and keep it from reflecting what it was made to show.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00452

The third is that the soul is turned away from the truth it needs to see. The souls of the righteous and obedient may be free from the dirt of wrongdoing and from deceit, yet still fail to see the truth clearly because they are not seeking it in depth. They have turned away from the path to the spiritual world—the careful study of true knowledge, reflection on God's signs, and awareness of His presence. Instead, they may focus all their effort on bodily acts, religious routines, and set prayers, without thinking about their meaning or purpose. They see only what they have set out to see: how to perform acts of worship correctly and avoid mistakes in prayer and other practices.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00453

If a person's fixed attention on good deeds can prevent a clear view of truth, then worldly desires and attachments will do so even more. In the mirror example, this is like turning the mirror away from the image. The fourth obstacle is a curtain placed between the soul and the truth. A person may control desire, seek knowledge, and think carefully, yet still fail to see what they seek because an accepted belief, learned in childhood and held on trust, blocks the truth from view. This is a major barrier for many theologians, sectarian loyalists, and even people known for learning and piety. Beliefs accepted without examination can take such a firm hold that they block the way to truth. In the mirror example, this is like a curtain placed between the mirror and the image.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00454

The fifth obstacle is not knowing which way to look for the truth. A learner cannot find the answer by any path at all. They need to recall what they already know and put the right ideas together in the right order. When they do this in the way used by careful thinkers, they find the right path and the answer becomes clear. The knowledge needed for happiness in the afterlife is not inborn. We reach it through earlier knowledge. Any new piece of knowledge depends on two earlier pieces being joined in a particular way, much as a child comes from the union of male and female. Every possible being has its own cause, and nothing that depends on a cause can come into being without it. In the same way, we can know a thing only by learning its causes. Not knowing the first principles or how to put them together blocks us from knowledge.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00455

In the mirror example, this is like not standing at the right angle to see the image. If someone wants to see the back of their head in a mirror, they need two mirrors. One is placed behind them and the other in front, so the first reflection appears in the second mirror. The mirrors must be set at just the right angle. The paths to knowledge are even more subtle. Few people on earth know how to follow them. These are the obstacles that keep the rational soul from knowing what things are. By its original nature, every soul is able to know the truth, because it is a noble, God-given reality, different from all other things in this world. The Prophet is reported to have said, “If devils did not circle around the hearts of the children of Adam, they would see the kingdom of the heavens.” This refers to the soul's natural capacity and to the barriers that block it from the spiritual world.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00456

When those barriers are lifted from the heart—the rational soul—the forms of the spiritual and material worlds appear within it. The soul then sees itself in a paradise as wide as the heavens and the earth, or even wider. The visible world is limited, but the spiritual world and its intellectual truths have no end. The visible and spiritual worlds together are called the Divine Presence, because God encompasses all that exists. What appears to the heart is, for some, paradise itself; for others, it is what earns them paradise. The breadth of their paradise depends on the breadth of their knowledge and on how much of God, His qualities, and His acts they come to see.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00457

All acts of worship and bodily practice aim to clear the heart, purify the soul, and improve its practical side. “Successful is the one who purifies it; lost is the one who corrupts it.” Purity alone is not true perfection, since it is the absence of something bad. The true aim is the light of faith: the knowledge of God, His acts, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day. God says, “When God wills to guide someone, He opens their heart to Islam, and they are in a light from their Lord.” An open heart is the goal of practical wisdom; light is the goal of theoretical wisdom. The true philosopher joins both. In the language of religion, such a person is a true believer. This is the great success.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00458
V. How the Active Intellect becomes present in our souls
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00459

The Active Intellect exists in itself, and it also exists in our souls. The soul reaches its full development when the Active Intellect is present within it, connected to it, and united with it. Nothing can be the natural goal of another thing unless the two can become one. What is a thing's natural goal at one time can become its form at another, unless something blocks its way. We explained this union in the general discussion of knowledge and the relationship between intellect and what it understands. That account is enough for those who can grasp it through insight and experience, though it will not help those who deny it. If someone asks how one thing can be both a cause that comes before another thing and a goal that follows it, they should return to the argument already given and follow the same path.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00460

We showed by proof and direct insight that the highest source is both the first and the last. Its being extends everywhere; its unity gathers everything; its light shines with full strength. All individual beings flow from it, and all that exists comes from it. Its complete being is the source of things and their goal and completion. It is the root and fruit of the tree of existence. Its unity is unlike other unities, which result when separate things are counted. Nothing is equal to its unity; nothing is like its existence. Its pure oneness gathers many things, runs through all unities, and its light reaches every being. As Imam Ali said, “He is with everything, but not by being joined to it; He is other than everything, but not by being apart from it.” Its existence as the source of all things does not rule out its also being their goal. All beings descend from it at the beginning and return to it in the end.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00461

The same is true, in their own way, of the beings of the sustaining lights and the separate divine forms. The Active Intellects are like rays of God's existence, and their unity reflects His unity. Their reach and completeness reflect His, though in a lesser way. They are the means by which things flow from God and return to Him. They are first in relation to the beings that come from them and last as the goal toward which those beings return. They exist through God's existence and remain through His permanence, like rays of His light and necessary expressions of His being.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00462

The Active Intellect's existence in itself is one question; its presence in our souls is another. We have already shown that it exists in itself. Now we ask how it completes the human soul. At first, the soul is already a soul, but its intellect is only a possibility. By understanding intellectual forms and learning to notice the ideas that follow from them, it can become an active intellect. It can then bring to mind what it knows whenever it wishes, without having to begin the work of learning all over again. It has moved from a possible intellect to an actual one.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00463

Whenever a capacity becomes real, something already capable of acting must bring about that change. If the cause were something nonintellectual, such as a body or a bodily power, then something lower in being would cause something higher. That would mean something other than intellect could produce intellect, which is impossible. If the cause is itself an intellect, then either it is an intellect by its original nature, or it too needs something else to make it actual. If so, we must ask the same question about that cause, leading to an endless chain. So there must be an intellect that is actual from the beginning: the Active Intellect, free of possibility and the weakness that comes with it.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00464

There is another way to show that it exists. A person may know something but not have it in mind at every moment. The knowledge is stored, and the person has the power to recall it. So the power to understand and the power to preserve knowledge are different: one receives knowledge, while the other keeps it. Since the soul receives, the source that preserves what it knows must be a higher being. This kind of being is the Active Intellect. It is clear that it cannot be a body or a power in a body, since neither can understand or be understood as an intellect does.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00465

Bodies affect other things through their position and contact. In spiritual beings, the matching relation is not physical nearness but a connection of meaning and intellect. God is the source of existence and gives it to every being able to receive it. But each kind of created thing also needs a fitting intermediary: a separate intellectual form or being. These are the close angels, called “lords of kinds” by the ancient philosophers, Platonic forms by the Platonists, and divine forms in this account. They are God's detailed knowledge of things, through which things beyond Him come to be. The intermediary most suited to completing human souls is their holy intellectual guide, called Gabriel and the Spirit of Holiness in religious teaching. In Persian, this being was called the Life-Giver. Several Qur'anic verses say that people and prophets receive knowledge from a powerful angel or from the All-Knowing through an angel.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00466

Sense images come to the imagination through the senses. From these images, the soul draws general meanings by noticing what things share and how they differ. At first, these meanings are vague and faint, like objects in a dark room. But as the soul grows ready through purification, freedom from inner stains, repeated perception, and careful thought, the Active Intellect's light shines on the soul and its imagined images. It makes the soul an actual intellect and its imagined ideas actual objects of thought.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00467

The Active Intellect acts on the soul and its images as the sun acts on a healthy eye and on the things before it. Before the sun rises, the eye can see only in potential, and the things around it can be seen only in potential. When sunlight reaches the eye, the eye actually sees and the things before it become visible. In the same way, when this sacred light reaches the soul and its imagined ideas, the soul becomes an actual intellect, able to think, and its imagined ideas become actual objects of thought. The intellect then distinguishes what is essential from what is accidental, what is real from what merely accompanies it, and what is basic from what follows from it. It understands these things apart from their numbers and individual instances. The human being then becomes an intellectual human being: its existence is no longer confined to separate bodily parts and attachments.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00468

As the light that forms the soul grows stronger, the soul unites with the universal human spirit, called the Spirit of Holiness and the Active Intellect. This source is wide enough to include all human beings, just as a universal nature can be said of many individuals. But the universal nature is only a general idea of those individuals, while this source is their real foundation: it contains them and keeps them. General natures, too, are signs of real, luminous beings and sacred intellectual forms. In short, when the soul becomes intellect, its sense images become actual objects of thought and are themselves known, for everything that is actually understood is also an actual knower.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00469
VI. The Anqa, the spiritual being of the mystics, described through symbols
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00470

The Anqa is a real being to the mystics. They are as certain of its existence as they are of whiteness. It is a sacred bird, and its home is Mount Qaf. Its whistle wakes those asleep in the beds of darkness. Its call stirs those who have forgotten God's signs, though few listen closely or recognize its echo. Many have shut themselves off from hearing and turned away from their Lord's signs. They are deaf, mute, and blind, so they do not understand. The Anqa is with all creation, though creation is not with it. As the Persian poet says:
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00471
You are with us, yet not one of us; you are beyond us, yet never apart.
Book Ten: The spiritual afterlife, intellectual happiness and misery, and other forms of happiness and misery
passage-en-00472

Anyone suffering from dropsy or an illness of black bile may drink from its shade. Those suffering from melancholy also benefit from hearing its call. Its wings and feathers have qualities that can heal many different illnesses and diseases. But there is one deadly illness it cannot heal: deep, stubborn ignorance. It can fly up and down without moving, and come and go without any change or journey. It can be near or far without distance or place. Colors appear through it, though it has no color; the same is true of tastes and smells. Whoever understands its language understands the languages of all birds and knows every truth and secret.
